newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Labour closes gap a week from election.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Labour closes gap a week from election.

text.p: New Zealand opposition Labour Party leader Helen Clark on Saturday hailed a newspaper opinion poll as evidence of a groundswell of support for her party, just a week away from a general election.
The poll, published on Saturday in the Auckland-based New Zealand Herald, shows a spectacular jump in support for Labour, up almost six points over a week to 27.7 percent.
Meanwhile, support for the ruling conservative National Party had dropped 2.8 points to 34 percent.
Clark said she had sensed a groundswell of support for Labour over the past month, which she put down largely to avoiding a negative campaigning style.
She said Labour was sticking to basic issues affecting ordinary New Zealanders and its message was being heard.

"We haven't tried to scare people, we have stuck to health, we have stuck to education, living standards for ordinary people, and we have given honest and frank answers to every policy question we've been asked. That's why I believe we're doing well," she told Radio New Zealand.

In the run-up to New Zealand's first election under proportional representation on October 12, the poll clearly showed that if the three main opposition parties were able to stitch together a coalition, they could form a government.

The New Zealand First Party was down four at 14 percent and the left-wing Alliance was up 0.6 points at 12.6 percent. The poll would give a Labour-New Zealand First-Alliance arrangement 73 seats in the 120 seat single chamber parliament.
It would also bring a Labour-New Zealand First or Labour- Alliance deal within striking distance of the 60 seats needed to command a majority.
National's likely coalition partners remained below the crucial five percent threshold at which parties which fail to win a constituency seat qualify for proportional representation in parliament.
The poll, which showed Clark doubling her personal ranking, was taken during a week which saw her emerge as the clear winner of the first televised political leaders debate.

Labour has gained five percentage points in each of the last two weekly surveys. National dropped nearly three points last week and another three points this week. If the trends continue, Labour could have its nose in front next Saturday night.
